questionText: What is the difference between an array and a List<T> in C#?
shortAnswer: Arrays have a fixed size set at creation; List<T> resizes dynamically, keeps a Count separate from Capacity, and offers Add/Remove/Insert. Prefer List<T> unless the size is truly fixed or you need multidimensional/unsafe interop shapes.
detailedAnswer: Arrays (int[] a = new int[4]) allocate one contiguous block whose Length never changes — 'resizing' means allocating a new array and copying (Array.Resize does exactly this). They are the most memory-efficient and interop-friendly shape, and the runtime applies bounds-check elimination in tight loops. List<T> wraps an array with a growth strategy: it doubles Capacity when Count would exceed it, so N appends cost O(N) total (amortized O(1) each) with at most ~2x transient waste. List<T> also gives AddRange, Insert, RemoveAt, Find, BinarySearch, Sort, and ForEach, plus TrimExcess to release spare capacity. Capacity vs Count is the key mental model: Capacity is the rented buffer, Count is the used portion — setting Capacity up front (new List<int>(10000)) avoids repeated doubling when the size is predictable. Collection expressions (C# 12: List<int> xs = [1, 2, 3];) work for both. For fixed-size hot loops, arrays or Span<T> over them win; for everything else, List<T> is the default.
internalWorking: List<T> holds a T[] field; growth allocates a new array (doubling, minimum 4) and Array.Copy's the contents. The old array becomes garbage — repeated growth in a loop is the classic Gen0 churn pattern. Arrays are SZ (single-dimension, zero-based) for the fast path; multidimensional arrays (int[,]) are slower due to complex indexing.
realWorldUsage: Method results and DTO collections are List<T> (or IReadOnlyList<T> for exposure); fixed buffers, pixel rows, and P/Invoke signatures use arrays; parsing pipelines slice arrays via Span<T>.
commonMistake: Pre-sizing confusion: new List<int>(10) sets Capacity, not Count — flex[0] still throws until Add is called. Also: exposing List<T> from APIs invites callers to mutate internal state; return IReadOnlyList<T> or AsReadOnly().
technicalConversation: Ask when they last set an initial capacity and why — predictable-size loads (CSV rows, DB result counts) are the textbook case, and the answer reveals whether they think about growth cost.
interviewFollowUp: What is the amortized cost of N Add operations, and where does the transient memory waste go?
keyTakeaway: Arrays = fixed, lean, fast. List<T> = array + doubling growth + rich API. Know Count vs Capacity.

questionText: How do List<T> Add, Insert, and RemoveAt perform, and what does that imply for usage?
shortAnswer: Add is amortized O(1) (occasional doubling copy); Insert/RemoveAt are O(n) because elements after the index shift. Implications: append freely, insert/remove in the middle sparingly, and prefer LinkedList<T> or index-keyed structures only when middle mutation dominates.
detailedAnswer: Add appends at Count and only copies when growth triggers (doubling keeps total copies O(N) across N adds). Insert(i, x) must shift every element from i right by one (Array.Copy inside) — O(n) time on every call, so inserting N items at the front is O(N^2). RemoveAt(i) shifts left similarly; Remove(x) first scans (O(n) Equals per element) then shifts. Clear() keeps the buffer (Count = 0, Capacity retained — reuse-friendly) while TrimExcess() shrinks to fit. For queue-like usage (dequeue from front repeatedly), List<T> is O(n) per dequeue — use Queue<T> (ring buffer, O(1)) instead. For frequent middle edits with stable iterators, LinkedList<T> gives O(1) insert/remove given the node, at the price of per-node allocations and cache-hostile traversal (arrays win scans by 5–10x via prefetching). Sorting is O(n log n) introsort via List.Sort (optionally with Comparison<T> or IComparer<T>). BinarySearch needs a sorted list and returns the bitwise complement of the insertion point when missing — a classic off-by-one source.
internalWorking: Insert/RemoveAt lower to Array.Copy (memmove) — fast per byte but linear in distance. List.Sort uses introspective sort (quicksort → heapsort fallback + insertion for small partitions). Queue<T> is a circular array with head/tail indices that doubles on wrap.
realWorldUsage: Append-mostly pipelines (collect then process) love List<T>; work queues use Queue<T>/Channel<T>; LRU caches pair Dictionary with LinkedList nodes; leaderboards sort once then BinarySearch.
commonMistake: Removing inside foreach (InvalidOperationException — iterate backwards by index or collect-then-remove), and using List<T> as a queue (O(n) dequeues that show up as CPU in profiles). Also: misreading BinarySearch negatives as 'not found at index -x' instead of complement.
technicalConversation: Ask them to design a log buffer with cap 10k, append-heavy, occasional eviction — the answer space (ring buffer vs List+RemoveRange vs Queue) exercises exactly these complexities.
interviewFollowUp: Why does Clear() keep Capacity, and when would you call TrimExcess()?
keyTakeaway: Append O(1), middle edits O(n). Match the structure to the mutation pattern, not just the element type.

questionText: What are collection expressions and spread syntax in C# 12, and when do they allocate?
shortAnswer: Collection expressions ([1, 2, 3], [..a, ..b]) build arrays, spans, or lists with one syntax; .. spreads another collection inline. They lower to the most efficient construction available (array init, builder, or Add loop) — no hidden magic, with spans staying stack-only.
detailedAnswer: Before C# 12 each target needed its own syntax (new[] {}, new List<int> {}, ToArray()). Collection expressions unify: int[] a = [1, 2, 3]; List<string> l = ["x"]; int[][] jagged = [[1], [2, 3]]; Span<int> s = [4, 5]; and int[] combined = [..a, ..b, 9]; (spread). The compiler picks the lowering by target: arrays → newarr + fill; List<T> → new + Add calls (or CopyTo fast path for spreads of known-size collections); Span<T> over inline data → compiler-generated static data blob + slice (zero allocation); ImmutableArray<T> → builder. Spread of an unknown-length IEnumerable falls back to enumeration + Add (one pass, no double-enumeration). Params collections (params int[] → params collections) let methods accept [1, 2] inline. Rules: no mixing target-typed new confusion — the target type must be a known collection shape; empty [] needs a target type; spread of null throws NullReferenceException (guard or ?? []... in an array context). Style: prefer collection expressions for literals and concatenation; keep explicit constructors where capacity or comparer configuration matters (e.g. new HashSet<string>(comparer) can't be expressed).
codeExample:
int[] a = [1, 2, 3];
List<int> l = [..a, 4, 5];      // spread + append
int[][] grid = [[1, 2], [3]];     // nested
Span<int> stack = [7, 8, 9];      // static data, no heap
string[] empty = [];              // needs target type
void Log(params List<string> ms) { } // params collections
Log(["a", "b"]);
internalWorking: The compiler emits InlineArray-style static data for constant spans (stored in the PE data section, loaded via pointer + length). Spreads over ICollection<T> use Count + CopyTo (single allocation, block copy); over bare IEnumerable they enumerate into a builder. No runtime helper beyond normal Add/CopyTo calls.
realWorldUsage: Test data, option lists, middleware branch maps, combining header collections, and stack-based parsing buffers without ArrayPool ceremony.
commonMistake: Spreading null ([..maybeNull] throws), assuming [] has a type (it doesn't — target required), and expecting comparer support (HashSet with OrdinalIgnoreCase still needs explicit construction).
technicalConversation: Ask what [..a, ..b] compiles to when a is List<int> vs IEnumerable<int> — Count+CopyTo versus enumerate-and-grow is the performance conversation.
interviewFollowUp: How does the compiler keep Span<int> s = [1,2,3] allocation-free, and what constraint does that place on the data?
keyTakeaway: One literal syntax for all collection shapes; the compiler picks the cheapest lowering. Spreads need non-null, spans need constants.

questionText: How does Dictionary<TKey, TValue> work, and what makes a good key?
shortAnswer: Dictionary hashes keys into buckets for O(1) average lookup/insert/delete. A good key is immutable with stable, well-distributed GetHashCode and value equality (IEquatable<T>) — plus an explicit IEqualityComparer<T> when the default comparison is wrong (e.g. case-insensitive strings).
detailedAnswer: Internally: an entries array (hash, next, key, value) plus a buckets array pointing at entry chains. Lookup hashes the key, mods into a bucket, then walks the chain comparing with the equality comparer. Average O(1); worst case O(n) when all keys collide (hash flooding — randomized string hashing mitigates attacks). Capacity grows by prime-number resizing; construct with capacity (new Dictionary<string, X>(8000)) and/or comparer up front for hot maps. Good keys: immutable (mutating a key corrupts its bucket position → lost entries), GetHashCode consistent with Equals (equal objects must hash equal), fast to hash (int/Guid are ideal; long strings cost per lookup). Custom structs as keys need IEquatable<T> + GetHashCode (else boxing on every probe). Comparers: StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase for headers/routes; custom IEqualityComparer<T> for composite or normalized keys (e.g. trimmed email). Access patterns: TryGetValue (single probe) over ContainsKey+indexer (double probe); GetValueOrDefault/CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault for counting loops; indexer set adds-or-updates (no duplicate-key throw — Add throws instead). Enumeration order is undefined — never depend on it; SortedDictionary/SortedList trade O(log n) for ordering.
internalWorking: Hash → bucket index via (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % bucketSize; collisions chain via entry.next indices (open addressing with chaining hybrid in modern .NET: entries array + bucket heads). Resize rehashes all entries into the next prime-sized table. StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase hashes case-folded spans without allocating.
realWorldUsage: Caches and indexes (id → entity), frequency counters, header bags, route tables, memoization, and grouping (or ToLookup/GroupBy for multi-value).
commonMistake: Mutable keys (DateTime-normalized? classes with settable fields) that silently vanish from the map; case-sensitive default for user input ("User" vs "user" duplicates); double-probe ContainsKey patterns in hot loops; depending on enumeration order.
technicalConversation: Ask what happens when GetHashCode is constant (return 0) — correctness survives (Equals chain) but every lookup degrades to O(n); the follow-up is how they would detect it (profiler showing Equals-dominated time).
interviewFollowUp: Why must equal objects have equal hash codes, but unequal objects may share one?
keyTakeaway: Hash once, probe O(1). Immutable keys, correct comparer, TryGetValue — and never trust ordering.

questionText: When should you use HashSet<T>, and how do set operations replace nested loops?
shortAnswer: HashSet<T> stores unique values with O(1) add/contains/remove. Its set operations (UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith, Overlaps, SetEquals, IsSubsetOf) replace O(n*m) nested-loop comparisons with hashed O(n+m) logic — for tags, permissions, dedup, and diffing.
detailedAnswer: Any 'is X in group' or 'which items differ' problem is a set problem: HashSet<T> answers Contains in O(1) versus List.Contains O(n). Construction dedups automatically (new HashSet<int>(ids)). Core ops mutate in place: UnionWith (add all), IntersectWith (keep common), ExceptWith (remove present), SymmetricExceptWith (toggle). Queries return bool: Overlaps (any common), SetEquals (same members), IsSubsetOf/IsProperSubsetOf, IsSupersetOf. LINQ mirrors them functionally (Union/Intersect/Except/Distinct) but allocates and defers — HashSet methods are in-place and allocation-free, better for repeated use; LINQ is better for one-shot queries. Comparers matter identically to Dictionary (StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase for tags). Capacity constructor avoids rehashing for known sizes. Versioning: modifying during enumeration throws (same as all BCL collections). For sorted uniqueness use SortedSet<T> (red-black tree, O(log n), ordered enumeration + Min/Max/GetViewBetween range views). For concurrent uniqueness, ConcurrentDictionary<T, byte> as a set (no ConcurrentHashSet exists — the byte-value trick) or lock around HashSet for low contention.
internalWorking: Same machinery as Dictionary (buckets + entries) without values. Set operations iterate the smaller set probing the larger. LINQ's Intersect builds an internal Set<T> (a HashSet equivalent) — same complexity, plus enumerator allocations.
realWorldUsage: Permission/role checks, tag filtering, import dedup, allow/block lists, diffing snapshots (added/removed IDs), and graph visited-sets (BFS/DFS).
commonMistake: List.Contains in a loop over large data (quadratic blowup — the #1 accidental O(n^2) in business code), forgetting the comparer for strings (case duplicates), and mutating a HashSet while enumerating it.
technicalConversation: Ask them to find the accidental quadratic in a recent codebase — nested Contains/Any over lists is almost always present somewhere, and the HashSet rewrite is the standard fix.
interviewFollowUp: How would you implement a concurrent unique set, given there is no ConcurrentHashSet<T>?
keyTakeaway: Membership and diffing are set problems. HashSet turns nested loops into hashed linear passes.

questionText: What is the difference between IEqualityComparer<T> and IEquatable<T>, and when do you write each?
shortAnswer: IEquatable<T> is implemented BY the type (its natural equality); IEqualityComparer<T> is implemented OUTSIDE the type (a pluggable comparison strategy passed to collections). Write IEquatable on value types you own; write IEqualityComparer when the type is external, sealed, or needs context-dependent comparison.
detailedAnswer: IEquatable<T>.Equals(T) defines what equality means for the type itself — implement it on structs/classes where value equality is intrinsic (Money, OrderId), together with Equals(object), GetHashCode, and == / !=. The BCL calls it from EqualityComparer<T>.Default, so Dictionary/HashSet/Contains pick it up automatically. IEqualityComparer<T> (Equals(x, y) + GetHashCode(obj)) is a strategy object you hand to a specific collection: StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase for dictionaries of user input, a trimmed-email comparer for dedup, an Id-only comparer for entities whose full equality is too strict for a cache. One type, many comparisons — that is the point: Money's natural equality (amount+currency) versus a cache keyed by amount alone. Rules: comparer GetHashCode must agree with its own Equals (same contract as ever); comparers should be stateless singletons (static readonly Instance or StringComparer's built-ins); never mutate comparison state per call. Records generate IEquatable<T> for free; custom comparers still apply where needed (e.g. record with case-insensitive name lookup). Testing: assert both directions (a.Equals(b) && comparer consistency) plus hash agreement on equal instances.
internalWorking: Collections store the comparer reference and call it per probe; the default comparer is a cached per-T singleton resolved once (GenericEqualityComparer vs Object fallback). A broken comparer (hash/equals mismatch) corrupts bucket placement — lookups miss existing keys with no exception, the nastiest silent bug in this area.
realWorldUsage: Case-insensitive route/header maps, tenant-normalized keys, test-specific lenient comparisons, and caches keyed by a subset of entity fields.
commonMistake: GetHashCode/Equals disagreement in custom comparers (silent lookup misses), stateful comparers (culture captured per instance), and implementing IEquatable but forgetting GetHashCode (Dictionary breaks while List.Contains works — confusing split).
technicalConversation: Ask why entities often need an Id-only comparer for caches but full equality for tests — same type, two valid equalities, which is exactly the strategy pattern's home turf.
interviewFollowUp: What breaks, observably, when a comparer's GetHashCode disagrees with its Equals?
keyTakeaway: IEquatable = the type's own equality; IEqualityComparer = pluggable per-collection strategy. Both must keep hash and equals in agreement.

questionText: What causes InvalidOperationException 'Collection was modified' and how do you avoid it?
shortAnswer: Enumerators snapshot a version stamp; any Add/Remove during foreach invalidates it and the next MoveNext throws. Avoid by iterating a copy (ToList), iterating backwards by index for removals, or collecting changes and applying after the loop.
detailedAnswer: Every BCL collection keeps an internal version incremented on structural change. GetEnumerator captures it; MoveNext compares and throws on mismatch — a fail-fast guard against skipped/duplicated elements, not a locking mechanism (it never made enumeration thread-safe). Patterns: (1) ToList()/ToArray() snapshot then mutate the original — simple, one allocation; (2) reverse for-loop for removals (indices below the cursor never shift); (3) collect-then-apply (var doomed = list.Where(...).ToList(); foreach remove); (4) RemoveAll(predicate) — single pass, no enumerator, fastest for List<T>; (5) dictionaries: collect keys first (dict.Keys.Where(...).ToList()) since even value updates via indexer... note: updating an existing value does NOT bump the version (safe), but Add/Remove does; (6) concurrent scenarios: ConcurrentDictionary/ConcurrentBag tolerate mutation during enumeration by design (snapshot or weakly-consistent semantics). LINQ defers execution — foreach over a query re-enumerates the source each time, so mutating inside can throw far from the cause or, worse, silently re-query. Fix by materializing (ToList) before the mutating loop. Immutable collections (ImmutableList<T>) sidestep entirely: every 'mutation' returns a new instance, enumerators never invalidate.
internalWorking: List<T>.Enumerator stores _version = list._version at creation; MoveNext checks equality (one int compare — negligible). Dictionary uses a generation counter covering Add/Remove/Clear (value overwrite via existing key does not increment). Concurrent collections use lock-free nodes/tables where iterators traverse snapshots or tolerate races by contract.
realWorldUsage: Pruning expired cache entries, filtering in-memory work queues, bulk-unsubscribing event handlers, and cleaning navigation collections in EF-tracked graphs.
commonMistake: Removing in foreach (the #1 beginner exception), 'fixing' it with ToList inside a hot loop (allocation per iteration — hoist the snapshot), and assuming the exception means threading (it usually means same-thread mutation).
technicalConversation: Ask whether the exception guarantees detection — no: version is an int that can theoretically wrap, and some paths (List.ForEach with external mutation) behave differently; it is a diagnostic aid, not a contract.
interviewFollowUp: Why is updating an existing dictionary value safe during enumeration while adding a key is not?
keyTakeaway: Enumerators are fail-fast version checks. Snapshot, reverse-index, or RemoveAll — never mutate inside foreach.

questionText: How do multidimensional arrays, jagged arrays, and spans compare for grid-like data?
shortAnswer: Jagged arrays (int[][]) are arrays of arrays — fastest in C# (SZ fast path, LINQ-friendly). Multidimensional (int[,]) is one block with slower indexing and no LINQ. For interop/performance, a flat 1D array + Span<T> slicing beats both on cache and flexibility.
detailedAnswer: int[,] rect = new int[rows, cols]: single allocation, GetLength(d) dimensions, but indexing compiles to a call (mult + bounds per dimension) and it doesn't implement IList<T> (no LINQ, awkward APIs). int[][] jagged: each row an independent SZ array — row lengths may vary, indexing is two fast SZ accesses, rows are individually passable to methods/Span, and it parallelizes naturally (Parallel.For over rows). Flat int[] data = new int[rows * cols] with idx = r * cols + c: best cache locality, single bounds check, sliceable via data.AsSpan(start, cols) for row views, resizable via Array.Resize, and directly pinnable for interop. Rule of thumb: jagged for idiomatic C# grids; flat+Span for performance/interop; multidimensional mostly for interop signatures and math-mirroring readability. Memory<T>/ArrayPool<T> back flat buffers in pipelines (rent, slice, return). Collection expressions build jagged grids neatly ([[1, 2], [3]]). Avoid List<List<T>> for numeric grids (double indirection + per-row objects); prefer arrays and expose IReadOnlyList views.
internalWorking: SZ array access is a single bounds check + pointer add (often eliminated in counted loops). Multidim access calls the runtime helper (address = base + (i0*len1 + i1)*size with per-dim checks). Flat spans keep one bounds check per slice, then unchecked interior access after JIT proof.
realWorldUsage: Image buffers (flat byte[] + spans), game boards, CSV matrices, numerical code, and GPU/interop staging buffers.
commonMistake: int[,] with LINQ attempts (doesn't implement IEnumerable<T>), jagged rows left null (NullReference on first access — initialize each row), and row-major vs column-major traversal (column-major on row-major data destroys prefetching — 10x slowdowns in tight loops).
technicalConversation: Ask them to predict the fastest traversal order and why — row-major inner loop matches allocation order, keeping cache lines hot; the profiler confirms via cache-miss counters.
interviewFollowUp: Why can the JIT eliminate bounds checks for flat arrays in counted for loops but not for int[,] access?
keyTakeaway: Jagged for idiom, flat+Span for speed, multidimensional rarely. Traverse in allocation order.

questionText: How do ToLookup and GroupBy differ, and when is a dictionary of lists the wrong tool?
shortAnswer: Both group by key; GroupBy defers (re-runs per enumeration), ToLookup executes immediately into an immutable multi-value map. A hand-built Dictionary<K, List<V>> needs null checks and is re-created per query — ToLookup/GroupBy express intent directly; use a persistent dictionary only for long-lived indexes.
detailedAnswer: var byDept =emps.GroupBy(e => e.Dept): deferred query — enumerating twice re-groups (and re-runs any database query twice with EF!). .ToLookup(e => e.Dept) materializes an ILookup<K,V>: indexer returns an empty sequence for missing keys (no KeyNotFoundException — convenient but hides typos), immutable, ideal for in-memory fan-out (parent → children rendering, batching by tenant). Dictionary<K,List<V>> built by hand: fine as a long-lived index (adjacency lists, caches), but for one-shot grouping it is ceremony with TryGetValue-or-create branches. With EF Core, GroupBy translates to SQL GROUP BY (server-side, efficient) while ToLookup forces client evaluation of the whole set first — choose by data size and location. Counting per group: GroupBy + Select(g => (g.Key, g.Count())) beats materializing groups. Nested grouping builds hierarchies (dept → team → people) in one pass. For streaming large inputs, Lookup's full materialization may OOM where a sorted-input single-pass grouping would not — know your data size. ILookup exposes Count per key and Contains(key); it has no Add — rebuild or use a mutable dictionary for evolving maps.
internalWorking: Lookup<TKey,TElement> hashes into groupings (arrays of key + elements) in one pass — O(n) build, O(1) key access. GroupBy uses deferred execution with its own internal lookup per enumeration. EF translates GroupBy+aggregates to GROUP BY; unaggregated GroupBy may client-evaluate (logged as warning — read your logs).
realWorldUsage: Rendering master-detail pages (order → lines), batching notifications by tenant, building nav trees, and test-result grouping in runners.
commonMistake: Enumerating a GroupBy twice (double work/double SQL), ToLookup on huge streams (memory), hand-rolled dict-of-lists with missing-key throws (use GetValueOrDefault or Lookup), and GroupBy in EF without aggregation causing client evaluation.
technicalConversation: Ask how they would render 10k orders with lines from one query — single query + ToLookup split in memory versus N+1 lazy loads is the ORM maturity test.
interviewFollowUp: Why does ILookup's indexer return empty instead of throwing, and when does that convenience hide bugs?
keyTakeaway: GroupBy = deferred query, ToLookup = immutable now-map, hand dict = long-lived index. Never N+1 what you can group once.

questionText: What collection should you expose from public APIs: List<T>, IEnumerable<T>, IReadOnlyList<T>, or array?
shortAnswer: Return the least powerful type that satisfies callers: IReadOnlyList<T>/IReadOnlyCollection<T> for in-memory results, IEnumerable<T> for streams/queries (with deferred-execution caveats), arrays for fixed interop shapes. Never return List<T> from a public API — it invites mutation of your internals.
detailedAnswer: The decision matrix: (1) Callers need indexing + Count → IReadOnlyList<T> (backed by List<T>/array, wrapped via AsReadOnly() for live views or ToList() for snapshots). (2) Forward-only, possibly lazy/infinite/streaming → IEnumerable<T> with documented single/multi enumeration semantics (yield methods + EF queries defer — document whether re-enumeration re-queries). (3) Fixed-size primitives for interop/serialization → arrays (JSON serializers love T[]). (4) Unique results → IReadOnlySet<T>/ISet<T>. Never expose List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>, or HashSet<T> fields/properties directly — callers Add/Clear your state (defensive copies or wrappers). Input parameters: accept the most general usable type (IEnumerable<T>/IReadOnlyCollection<T>/ReadOnlySpan<T>) so callers pass arrays, lists, or LINQ freely; avoid List<T> parameters (forces callers to materialize). Count checks: prefer TryGetNonEnumeratedCount / Any() over Count() == 0 (avoids full enumeration). Async streams: IAsyncEnumerable<T> for paged/large flows with await foreach + cancellation. Records/DTOs: init IReadOnlyList<T> properties (NonNull + empty, never null — return Array.Empty<T>() instead of null).
internalWorking: Interface dispatch costs nothing measurable versus concrete calls after JIT devirtualization of sealed paths; ToList() allocates once (right-sized when source exposes Count via TryGetNonEnumeratedCount). AsReadOnly() wraps without copying (live view — mutations reflect; choose snapshot vs view deliberately).
realWorldUsage: Repository/service return types, SDK design (HttpClient returns HttpResponseMessage, content as streams), minimal-API results, and library surfaces reviewed for breaking-change safety (returning concrete List today blocks switching to a lazy stream tomorrow).
commonMistake: Null collections (return empty, never null), multiple enumeration of expensive IEnumerables (materialize or document), List<T> properties on DTOs that serializers then mutate, and IQueryable leaking past repositories (query logic escapes to callers).
technicalConversation: Ask them to review a method returning List<T> built from EF — the talking points (mutation, deferred intent, IQueryable leak risk) reveal API-design maturity.
interviewFollowUp: When is IEnumerable<T> the wrong return type even though it is the most general?
keyTakeaway: Return read-only minimums, accept general maximums, never null, never mutable internals. Types are API promises.
